title: The parrot drops
hook: hearing the caged parrot's words, a wild parrot falls as if dead, and the merchant reports it home (Masnavi 1)

segments.voice: Last week ended with a caged parrot asking the merchant to carry a greeting to the free parrots of India: greet them for me. Now a new week begins.

You send a text you think is harmless. A joke, a bit of news, a passing comment. Then the little dots appear, and disappear, and appear again, and you realize, too late, that your words landed like a stone. Words can do things no one meant them to do. The merchant arrives in India. He finds the forests, and the parrots flashing green in the trees. And, faithful to his promise, he delivers his parrot's message. Today, the parrot drops.
screen: `A HARMLESS TEXT LANDS LIKE A STONE.` → `THE FORESTS OF INDIA.` → `THE PARROT DROPS.`

segments.voice: He stands under the trees and repeats his parrot's words exactly: a parrot who loves you is shut in a cage in my house; is it right that it wastes away while you fly free? As soon as he's finished, one of the wild parrots begins to tremble. It shakes, loses its grip, and falls from the branch to the ground. Still. As if dead. The merchant is horrified. What have I done? I've killed a creature with a sentence. Maybe this bird and mine were kin, as close as body and soul. Why did I ever carry that message? Rumi stops here to reflect. Words, he says, are like flint and steel: what springs from the tongue is fire. Once spoken, they're an arrow already shot; you can't call them back. They travel, and they do things in the world, often things you didn't intend. So guard your tongue. But there's another side. Those words did something no gift could have done. They moved a wild bird so deeply it fell from the tree, because words reach inside. The merchant finishes his trading, sad, and goes home. He hands out the gifts. Then the parrot in its cage says: and my gift? What did you see? What did you say? The merchant doesn't want to answer. He's ashamed, and he knows the story will hurt. But he tells it. What those words do next is tomorrow's story. For today: every message does something.
screen: `HIS PARROT'S WORDS, EXACTLY.` · `A WILD PARROT FALLS, AS IF DEAD.` · `WORDS ARE FIRE, AN ARROW SHOT.` · `AND MY GIFT? WHAT DID YOU SAY?` · then, large: `EVERY MESSAGE DOES SOMETHING.`

segments.voice: Think back to a message that changed your day: good news, bad news, a single sentence from someone. Where were you, and what happened in your body when you heard it? Then recall one you sent that did more than you expected, for good or for ill, and just notice the power running both ways.
Arrow. Rumi's image for a spoken word: once loosed, like an arrow already shot, it can't be called back. Today's word.
Your line: what the message did. Once spoken, words travel, and they act. Back tomorrow.

howItsDone: Teachers of the Masnavi often pause at this scene to discuss Rumi's reflections on speech, that words spoken cannot be taken back, before continuing the parrot's story.
